planting.note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; because Rubel is a direct wild selection rather than a bred hybrid, plant it alongside a compatible modern highbush variety such as Bluecrop or Jersey to ensure strong cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Set container or bare-root plants into acidic, peat- or pine-bark-amended soil in early spring, spacing plants to allow for a dense, twiggy, upright habit, and mulch heavily to conserve the constant moisture this variety needs while establishing. Rubel traces back to a single wild bush found in 1912 in the New Jersey Pine Barrens by a woodsman named Rube Leek, one of the hundreds of wild bushes Elizabeth Coleman White paid local woodsmen to locate for her and Frederick Coville's pioneering blueberry domestication project; its name is a portmanteau of 'Rube' and 'Leek.' Unlike most modern highbush cultivars, Rubel was never hybridized — it is a direct wild-type selection — and it produces smaller, intensely flavored, true 'wild blueberry' tasting fruit in abundant clusters on a vigorous, twiggy, upright-to-spreading bush that colors brilliant red-orange in fall. It remains in commercial production over a century later and sits at the root of the pedigree of nearly every modern highbush cultivar.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; pair with another midseason-to-late highbush variety for cross-pollination, and expect a somewhat lower-vigor, less heavily-cropping bush than workhorse commercial cultivars in exchange for exceptional dessert quality.

directions: Site plants in consistently moist, acidic soil in full sun and mulch with pine bark or pine straw, since Elizabeth is a lower-vigor grower that rewards attentive care with some of the best-flavored fruit of any highbush cultivar. Named for Elizabeth Coleman White, the New Jersey cranberry grower who partnered with USDA botanist Frederick Coville to domesticate the highbush blueberry in the early twentieth century, this variety fell into relative obscurity for decades before flavor-focused trials in the early 2000s brought it back into cultivation, where tasting panels have repeatedly ranked it among the finest-flavored blueberries available, rivaling or exceeding favorites like Blueray. The large, sweet, well-balanced berries ripen midseason on a moderately vigorous, upright bush, making it a rewarding choice for home growers who prioritize eating quality over heavy commercial yields.
sources: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station / Rutgers

planting.note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Darrow is a vigorous, high-chill variety best suited to colder zones than the Gulf Coast, and benefits from cross-pollination with another late-season highbush cultivar such as Elliott or Jersey.

directions: Plant into acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun, spacing bushes generously to accommodate a vigorous, upright habit, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and evenly moist through the growing season. Released in 1965 through the cooperative USDA and New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program and named for USDA small-fruit breeder George M. Darrow, this cultivar was selected for exceptionally large, firm, dark-blue, high-dessert-quality berries and a very late ripening window that extends the highbush harvest after most other varieties have finished. Darrow requires a substantial chill period, making it best suited to cold-winter regions rather than the Deep South, but it remains valued in its home range for its combination of outsized fruit, good disease tolerance, and reliable late-season production.
sources: USDA / New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Liberty pairs well with its sibling releases Aurora and Draper for an extended, overlapping late-season harvest window and reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Plant into acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun with generous spacing for a tall, upright bush, and mulch well to maintain the even moisture this variety needs for best fruit quality. Bred at Michigan State University from a cross of Brigitta and Elliott, Liberty was selected in 1997 for improved flavor and fruit quality over the older Elliott variety and was commercially released in 2004 alongside its siblings Aurora and Draper — the trio that together became some of the most widely planted northern highbush blueberry cultivars in the world. Liberty ripens late in the season just ahead of Elliott, producing firm, light-blue, good-flavored berries on a vigorous, productive bush, and its late timing makes it valuable for extending the fresh blueberry harvest window in home plantings.
sources: Michigan State University Department of Horticulture
